'''Bruce Thomas Draine''' (born November 19, 1947, in [[Kolkata]]) is an American astrophysicist.<ref>{{Cite book |url= |title=American Men & Women of Science: A Biographical Directory of Today's Leaders in Physical, Biological, and Related Sciences |title-link=American Men and Women of Science |publisher=[[Gale (publisher)|Gale]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-0-02-866695-2 |editor-last=Nemeh |editor-first=Katherine H. |edition=38th |volume=4 |location=Farmington Hills, Michigan |pages=2902 |language=en |oclc=1152235791}}</ref> He is Professor of Astrophysical Sciences at [[Princeton University]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Bruce Draine |url=https://web.astro.princeton.edu/people/bruce-draine |access-date=2023-02-28 |website=Department of Astrophysical Sciences |publisher=[[Princeton University]] |language=en}}</ref>

He attended [[Swarthmore College]] from 1965 to 1969. He served in the [[U.S. Peace Corps]] in Ghana from 1969 to 1971, where he taught secondary school physics and mathematics. He received his Ph.D. from [[Cornell University]] in 1978. From 1979 to 1982 he was in the School of Natural Sciences at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>{{Cite web |date= 9 December 2019|title=Bruce Draine |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/bruce-draine |access-date=2023-02-28 |website=[[Institute for Advanced Study]] |language=en}}</ref> He is currently an emeritus professor in the Department of Astrophysical Sciences at Princeton University. His research involves the study of the [[interstellar medium]], especially [[cosmic dust|interstellar dust]], [[photodissociation region]]s, and [[Shock waves in astrophysics|interstellar shock waves]].<ref name=":0" /> 
[[File:At Princeton University 2024 058 - Bruce T. Draine.jpg|thumb|left|Draine at his desk in 2024]]
He is one of the authors (together with [[Piotr Flatau|Piotr J. Flatau]]) of the public domain [[DDSCAT]] code based on the [[discrete dipole approximation]] which has application to light scattering by non-spherical particles and nanophotonics.

==Honors and awards==
In 2004 he won the [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Astrophysics]] for his "fundamental, pioneering studies of interstellar processes".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dannie Heineman Prize for Astrophysics |url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/dannie-heineman-prize-astrophysics |access-date=2023-02-28 |website=[[American Astronomical Society]] |language=en}}</ref> In 2007, he was inducted into the [[National Academy of Sciences]] for his work in the field of Astrophysics. He was elected a Legacy Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]] in 2020.<ref>{{cite web |title=AAS Fellows |url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/aas-fellows |accessdate=27 September 2020 |website=[[American Astronomical Society]] |publisher=}}</ref>
